Breath of Life
BRETH uv LYFE
n. phr. (the breath God breathed into man, and the life-principle of all living creatures)
Hebrew nishmath chayyim in Genesis 2:7, from neshamah, breath or spirit, and chayyim, lives; and ruach chayyim in Genesis 6:17, from ruach, wind, breath, or spirit.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

The phrase enters Scripture at the making of man: “And the LORD God formed man of the dust of the ground, and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life; and man became a living soul.” Two actions are distinguished and both are necessary. The forming is of dust, which man shares with the beasts and the ground he was taken from; the breathing is direct, personal, and into the nostrils, and it is what makes the formed dust a living soul. The Authorized Version uses the same English phrase for the wider animal creation in the flood narrative — God destroys “all flesh, wherein is the breath of life”, and “All in whose nostrils was the breath of life, of all that was in the dry land, died” — so that the phrase names the life-principle of every breathing creature. The distinctive thing about man is not therefore that he breathes but the manner of his receiving: of no beast is it said that God breathed into his nostrils. Elihu states the doctrine plainly: “The Spirit of God hath made me, and the breath of the Almighty hath given me life.” The breath is given and is not owned. Scripture presses this: God “takest away their breath, they die, and return to their dust”, which means that every creature's continuance is a moment-by-moment loan. Life is not a possession secured at the beginning but a gift sustained, and it returns when He recalls it.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828): Breath, the air inhaled and expelled in respiration; life. The breath of life, Genesis 2:7, that which God breathed into man's nostrils, whereby he became a living soul.

expand to see more

Breath, the air inhaled and expelled in the respiration of animals.

Life; the power of breathing, and therefore of living.

Hebrew neshamah, breath, used of the breath God breathed into man.

Hebrew ruach, wind, breath, spirit, used of the breath of life in all flesh.

God breathed into his nostrils the breath of life, Genesis 2:7.

Key Scripture

Gen 2:7 — "And the LORD God formed man of the dust of the ground, and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life; and man became a living soul."

Gen 6:17 — "And, behold, I, even I, do bring a flood of waters upon the earth, to destroy all flesh, wherein is the breath of life, from under heaven; and every thing that is in the earth shall die."

Gen 7:22 — "All in whose nostrils was the breath of life, of all that was in the dry land, died."

Job 33:4 — "The Spirit of God hath made me, and the breath of the Almighty hath given me life."

Modern Corruption

Life is reduced to a chemical process that arose without a giver, and the breathing into the nostrils — the ground of human dignity and of the body's goodness — is lost with it.

expand to see more

Modern materialism holds that life is an arrangement of matter arrived at without intention, so that the difference between a living man and a dead one is a difference of chemistry and nothing further. Everything in Genesis 2:7 contradicts this, and the consequences are not abstract. If the breath is not given, it is not owed back, and no account can be given of why a life should be held sacred rather than useful. The doctrine that God breathed into man's nostrils is the foundation under the prohibition of murder in Genesis 9:6, and a culture that has let go of the former will not long keep the latter. Scripture's claim is that the breath in every man is on loan from the God who takes it away and who will require it.

A second and opposite error is older and runs through much popular Christian speech: the body is treated as a container and the real man as the breath inside it, so that salvation becomes escape from the flesh and the resurrection of the body is quietly dropped. Genesis will not have this either. Man does not receive a soul and keep it in a body; the formed dust plus the breathed breath becomes a living soul, and the whole man is what is meant. This is why the Christian hope is resurrection and not the immortality of a disembodied spirit, and why the body is called the temple of the Holy Ghost. The principle to recover is the unity of the man God made: dust that God breathed into, honourable in both halves, and owing every breath to the One who gave it.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew neshamah, breath; ruach, wind, breath, spirit; chayyim, lives; the life-principle given by God and recalled by Him.

expand to see more

Hebrew neshamah, breath, the word of Genesis 2:7.

Hebrew ruach, wind, breath, or spirit, used in Genesis 6:17.

Hebrew chayyim, lives, plural in form, rendered life.

Breathed into his nostrils, a direct and personal act toward man alone.

Used also of the beasts that breathe, Genesis 7:22.

Usage

"breathed into his nostrils the breath of life"

"all flesh, wherein is the breath of life"

"All in whose nostrils was the breath of life"
